overview: The Mamluk sultanate centred on Cairo and governed Egypt and much of Syria. Rulers drawn from military households supported institutions and specialised crafts. Surviving buildings and objects illuminate urban services, skilled labour, trade and the public display of authority.

periods.title: The Bahri period
periods.summary: Military households replaced Ayyubid rule in Egypt. Cairo became a centre of patronage, with religious, educational and charitable buildings supported by powerful rulers and officials.

periods.title: The Burji period
periods.summary: Later sultans continued commissioning architecture and luxury goods despite recurring political and economic difficulties. These phase labels describe ruling arrangements, not every inhabitant’s origin.

periods.title: Tuman Bey’s succession
periods.summary: After al-Ghawri died fighting the Ottomans in Syria, Tuman Bey became sultan in Egypt and resisted the advancing Ottoman army.

items.text: Military recruits entered the ruling system through enslavement, education and training, followed by manumission and service. Advancement was not solely hereditary. This path to elite office depended on coercive recruitment and should not be confused with freedom from social hierarchy.

Trade in silks and spices helped finance patronage. Textiles and carpets also circulated internationally. Skilled production connected merchants and workshops with wealthy buyers well beyond the sultanate.

Qalawun’s complex on Cairo’s al-Mu’izz Street joined a school, mosque, tomb and hospital. The arrangement brought teaching and care into an architectural foundation that also preserved the ruler’s memory. The building’s functions were broader than royal burial alone.

Shaykhu’s sabil, established in 1354, supplied water to passers-by. Its rock-cut rooms have openings to cisterns below, and jars were used in distribution. The surviving structure shows how storage and service worked together in a city street.

Qayitbay’s fifteenth-century complex combined a madrasa, a public water facility and a kuttab for Qur’anic teaching to poor Muslims. A courtyard and surrounding halls organised the school. Education, water supply and commemoration shared one foundation.

Wooden furnishings at Qayitbay’s madrasa include a pulpit and a Qur’an reciter’s chair inlaid with ivory. Their construction demonstrates skilled joinery and ornament in objects used for teaching and worship, alongside the stonework of the building.

sections.title: Crafts that carry names and meanings

items.text: A glass lamp made for Amir Qawsun around 1329 to 1335 combines a blown body and applied foot with enamel and gilding. Its inscription identifies the patron. The museum regards a mosque or tomb-hospice as its probable destination, rather than a proven findspot.

A fourteenth-century tray stand bears a cup emblem and an inscription naming Husain, son of Qawsun. Brass was worked and inlaid with contrasting metals. Stands of this kind held trays of fruit and other food, connecting elite dining with symbols of court office.

The Five Medallion Carpet, dated around 1500, uses wool for its foundation threads and knotted surface. Repeated geometric forms organise the long design. Its attribution to Egypt, probably Cairo, remains an attribution, not a documented excavation location.

A fifteenth-century engraved brass box names Muhammad al-Hamawi, the timekeeper at Damascus’s Umayyad Mosque. His office supervised prayer times and announcements concerning Ramadan. The box probably held food; it documents a specialist’s role without itself being a timekeeping instrument.

ending.text: Ottoman conquest ended the Egyptian sultanate in 1517. Tuman Bey was captured and executed in Cairo after resisting the invasion. Mamluk elites retained influence under Ottoman rule, so the loss of the sultanate did not immediately eliminate its military households or social power.
